text: In the Republic, education begins with stories, since children hear stories before they ever train their bodies (Book II, 376e–377a). The founders of the city must therefore supervise the makers of stories, and Socrates lays down two laws for what may be said about the gods. The first is that God is good, and for that reason the cause of good things only (379b–c). Nothing good can do harm. The evils of the world far outnumber the goods, and some other cause must be found for them. The second law is that God does not change and does not deceive (380d–381e). Whatever is in the best condition is least altered from outside, and a perfect being would never willingly change for the worse. These laws exclude a good deal of the inherited poetry: Homer's two jars standing at the threshold of Zeus (379d), every poet who blames a god for the ruin of a house, and the shape-shifting gods of the old stories. There are two kinds of lie, the spoken kind and the kind lodged in the soul, and gods and human beings hate the second most (382a–b). Socrates describes it as being deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself. A god has no such lie within and no motive to plant one in anyone else.
